extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, media students, and anyone interested in journalism ethics and newsroom accountability
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and failing modes for straight news reporting and newsroom oversight, as illustrated by the Jayson Blair fabrication and plagiarism scandal. Useful for evaluating reporter accuracy, sourcing, attribution, and editorial accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabrication (making up facts, quotes, events)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article documents multiple instances where the reporter fabricated facts, quotations, and events — e.g., claiming to have seen or interviewed people he never met, inventing a videotape, and fabricating details such as a 'dream' attributed to a source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: claiming quotes or observations that cannot be corroborated; inventing interactions or physical evidence (example: describing a videotape that did not exist). Examples from the page: Blair 'fabricated quotations from a person he had never interviewed', 'No such tape existed', and fabricating a dream he claimed a source had had. Best practice: only publish verifiable facts and accurately attribute quotations; do not invent details to strengthen a narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism (copying others' writing/quotes without attribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The page identifies numerous instances where text and quotations were copied from other outlets (Washington Post, Associated Press, The Plain Dealer, New York Daily News, San Antonio Express-News) without proper attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: close similarity to previously published stories, lifting quotations or phrasing without attribution (example: Blair's pieces contained plagiarized quotations from The Washington Post and AP). Best practice: attribute paraphrase and direct quotes to original sources and avoid reusing other outlets' language without clear credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline and location accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporter must not claim to have been physically present in the datelined location if they were not — the article recounts Blair 'claimed to have traveled to the city mentioned in the dateline, when in fact he did not.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: filing stories 'from' a city when reporting was done remotely or based on secondary sources. Example failures: claiming to be in Washington, Fairfax, Cleveland, Palestine (WV) when he had not traveled there. Best practice: only use a dateline for locations where reporting/observation actually occurred; clearly disclose remote reporting when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate attribution of sources (named and unnamed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Properly attribute statements and avoid inventing or misattributing witnesses or officials — e.g., Blair named lawyers who were not present and quoted 'unnamed officials' about a confession that everyone denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: attributing quotes to people who deny having said them or naming witnesses who were not present. Guidance: verify a source's presence and consent to quotation; be cautious with unnamed sources and ensure editors corroborate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respecting off-the-record agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not publish information that was promised to be 'off the record' — the article notes Blair 'published information that he had promised was off the record.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: breaking off-the-record commitments. Best practice: clearly establish and honor the terms of on/off-the-record conversations and document permissions for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of documentary/physical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm existence and content of physical evidence before reporting it (example: Blair described a videotape of Lee Malvo being questioned when no such tape existed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: reporting the existence or content of tapes, documents, or other artifacts without verification. Best practice: independently confirm the existence of materials and consult custodians or experts who can corroborate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate depiction of interviewees' circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not invent or exaggerate personal details about sources (examples: misreporting injuries, inventing amputations, mischaracterizing family circumstances, misspelling names, assigning attributes the person denied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: attributing medical prognosis or family facts that are false (example: saying a soldier 'will most likely limp the rest of his life' when untrue). Best practice: verify personal and medical details with reliable documentation or confirmed statements from the individuals involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding recycling/rearranging others' reporting as original reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting rearranged details or reworked material from wire services or other outlets as original contribution is misleading — the page notes Blair's 'entire contribution... consisted of rearranged details from Associated Press stories.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: repackaging other outlets' copy without new reporting or attribution. Best practice: disclose when material is derived from wire services or other reporting and add original reporting/corroboration if presenting it as original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration and use of multiple sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims — especially extraordinary ones — require corroboration; Blair's reliance on unverified claims and single-source assertions led to multiple falsehoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: relying on a single unverified source for central facts. Best practice: seek independent corroboration for key facts, especially in criminal cases or emotionally charged stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial oversight, investigation, and correction
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations must investigate credible allegations of reporter misconduct and publicly correct the record; The New York Times ran an extensive front-page investigation ('Correcting the Record') and followed with internal inquiries and editor resignations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: a newsroom should have procedures for investigating reporters' work, issuing corrections and transparent accounts of failures. Anti-patterns: ignoring staff warnings or failing to act on credible concerns (example: former Diamondback staffers alleged warnings were ignored). The page documents consequences including editors' resignations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about hiring, promotion, and newsroom practices when assessing failures
rubrics_metrics.description: When misconduct occurs, newsrooms should examine hiring and promotion processes (the Siegal committee found debate over affirmative action and whether race played a role in Blair's promotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: investigations into reporting failures should consider managerial decisions and systemic practices, while avoiding simplistic attributions. Anti-patterns: using individual misconduct to scapegoat or attack diversity efforts without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public accountability and disclosure of the extent of deception
rubrics_metrics.description: When widespread deception is discovered, organizations should disclose its extent and context to readers — exemplified by the NYT's 7,239-word front-page story detailing the 'long trail of deception.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: comprehensive, front-facing corrections and explanations of how failures occurred and what steps are being taken to prevent recurrence. Anti-patterns: minimal or buried corrections that do not fully inform the public.
